notes.meaning: Wisdom is described as a generous host who builds a grand, sturdy home. Her seven carved pillars show that her house is complete, strong, and lacks nothing. She creates a safe and lasting place where guests can come to learn and thrive.

differ.view: Wisdom represents Jesus Christ building His church, and the pillars represent the patriarchs, prophets, apostles, and pastors who uphold the truth.
Christ is Wisdom building His church, and the pillars are faithful gospel ministers who stand firm like the pillars in Solomon's temple.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Early and medieval teachers often interpreted Wisdom's house as Christ's human body and the seven pillars as the seven sacraments or the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: The seven pillars describe the typical architectural design of a large courtyard home or banquet pavilion in the ancient Near East.

notes.meaning: Wisdom prepares a rich feast of meat and carefully mixes her wine before setting her banquet table. In ancient times, hosts mixed wine with spices for rich flavor or diluted it with water for healthy drinking. God generously provides everything we need for spiritual health and joyful living.

Wisdom sends out her servant girls to invite guests, calling aloud from the highest spots in the city. High ridges and flat rooftops were the normal places to shout public news so everyone could hear. God makes His offer of guidance openly and clearly to all people.

Wisdom invites the simple and anyone who lacks good sense to turn aside and enter her home. These simple people are not hardened enemies of God, but young or inexperienced travelers who are still deciding how to live. God welcomes anyone who is humble enough to admit their need for direction.

Wisdom welcomes her guests to eat her bread and drink the wine she has prepared. This meal represents taking in God's truthful words and obeying His guidance. Feeding our souls on God's truth gives us strength for daily life just like bread fuels our bodies.

other.label: Catholic and Orthodox
other.view: The bread and mixed wine prefigure the sacrament of the Eucharist (the Lord's Supper), where believers feed spiritually on the body and blood of Christ.

notes.meaning: Guests must leave behind their foolish ways and silly companions if they want to live and find true understanding. A person cannot enjoy Wisdom's feast while still clinging to dangerous habits and corrupt friends. Walking with God means turning our backs on the things that drag us down.

Correcting a scorner only brings insults and shame back on the person trying to help. A scorner is someone who mocks holy things and refuses to listen to moral instruction. Wisdom reminds us that trying to correct an obstinate mocker is often useless and painful.

Rebuking a mocker will only make him hate you, but correcting a wise person will make them love you. Wise people know they are not perfect, so they appreciate helpful criticism that keeps them on the right path. Being willing to learn from correction is a sure sign of a teachable heart.

Giving instruction to a wise person makes them even wiser, and teaching a righteous person helps them grow in knowledge. Teachable people are like bees that gather sweetness from every flower they touch. When we have a humble attitude, every lesson helps us walk closer with God.

True wisdom begins with the fear of the Lord, which means honoring God with deep awe, reverence, and respect. Real understanding comes from knowing the Holy One and learning His will. No one can become truly wise without placing God at the center of their thoughts.

Wisdom adds length to a person's days and increases the years of their life. Living sensibly by God's rules helps protect our bodies and minds from the early ruin caused by reckless sins. God's truth brings both peace and protection to those who follow it.

Choosing wisdom brings great personal reward to the one who obeys, while choosing to mock brings trouble that the scorner must carry alone. Every individual must make their own personal decision between good and evil. We cannot blame others when we refuse God's good advice.

A foolish woman named Folly is shown as loud, reckless, and completely ignorant. She makes a lot of noise to get attention, but she has nothing good or sensible to say. Sin often uses loud, flashy appeals to hide the fact that it is completely empty inside.

Folly sits lazily at the doorway of her house on a prominent seat in the highest part of the city. Unlike Wisdom, who worked hard to prepare a feast, Folly acts like an arrogant queen waiting for victims. She stations herself where she can be noticed by as many people as possible.

Folly shouts out to everyday travelers who are walking straight ahead on their journeys. She deliberately targets innocent people minding their own business in order to pull them off the right road. Temptation always tries to distract us when we are trying to do what is right.

Folly uses the exact same invitation that Wisdom used, calling out to the simple and those lacking good judgment. She mimics the language of goodness to trick people who have not yet learned how to discern evil. Deceit often dresses up in familiar, friendly words to lure unsuspecting souls.

Folly whispers that stolen water is sweeter and secret bread tastes much better. She plays on sinful human nature, which wrongly craves whatever is forbidden and hidden. Secret sins promise deep excitement, but they only deliver guilt and trouble.

Those who step into Folly's house do not realize that previous visitors are already dead, resting in the depths of the grave (Sheol). Her promises of secret pleasure mask spiritual destruction and physical death. Walking into willful sin is like walking into a graveyard without knowing it.
